questions.question: Which Native American culture, known for building large earthen mounds and organizing society into chiefdoms, lived in Georgia when Europeans first arrived?
questions.correctAnswer: The Mississippian culture
distractors: The Paleo culture
The Archaic culture
The Woodland culture
questions.explanation: The Mississippians (about 800-1600 CE) were Georgia's most advanced prehistoric culture. Led by powerful chiefs, they built towns around temple mounds such as Etowah and Ocmulgee and farmed on a large scale.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Mound builders with chiefs - that is the Mississippians!

questions.question: How did growing maize (corn), beans, and squash help Mississippian chiefdoms grow into large, organized towns?
questions.correctAnswer: Farming produced a surplus of food, so some people could specialize in crafts, trade, and leadership instead of only hunting and gathering
distractors: The crops were traded to Europeans for metal tools and guns
The crops scared away rival groups and ended warfare
The three crops required no work, so everyone became a chief
questions.explanation: A reliable food surplus is what made Mississippian towns possible. With stored maize, beans, and squash, communities could support chiefs, priests, and skilled artisans, and store food for ceremonies and hard seasons.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Extra food builds towns - surplus first, specialists second!

img.tip: A food surplus let Mississippians specialize and build towns.

questions.question: What was the most devastating effect of Hernando de Soto's expedition through Georgia in 1540?
questions.correctAnswer: European diseases and violence devastated the Mississippian chiefdoms, which collapsed over the following century
distractors: De Soto founded the city of Savannah and made it a Spanish port
De Soto taught the Mississippians to grow cotton for export
De Soto signed a lasting peace treaty uniting all the chiefdoms
questions.explanation: De Soto's army marched across Georgia in 1540 taking food and captives. Worse, smallpox and other European diseases spread through towns that had no immunity, killing huge numbers of people and breaking the chiefdoms apart.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: De Soto brought disease, and the chiefdoms fell.

img.tip: De Soto's march spread disease that shattered the chiefdoms.

questions.question: Before the English founded Georgia, what did Spain build along Georgia's coast and barrier islands?
questions.correctAnswer: A chain of Catholic missions among the coastal Native Americans
distractors: A line of cotton plantations worked by enslaved Africans
Stone forts guarding a gold-mining district
Trading posts for the fur trade with Canada
questions.explanation: From the 1560s, Spanish Franciscan friars built missions among the Guale and Mocama peoples of the coast and barrier islands. Spain used the missions to claim the region and convert Native peoples long before England arrived.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Before the English, Spain planted missions on the coast.

questions.question: In 1732, King George II granted the charter for the colony of Georgia to whom?
questions.correctAnswer: A group of trustees led by James Oglethorpe
distractors: The Virginia Company of London
A single royal governor appointed for life
The Salzburgers of Ebenezer
questions.explanation: The Charter of 1732 put Georgia under 21 Trustees for 21 years. James Oglethorpe, a member of Parliament who fought for prison reform, was the group's driving force and the only Trustee who actually sailed to the colony.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Trustees ran Georgia first - Oglethorpe led them.

questions.question: Which three reasons explain why England founded Georgia?
questions.correctAnswer: To give the poor a fresh start, to produce goods such as silk and wine for England, and to form a military buffer protecting South Carolina from Spanish Florida
distractors: To grow cotton with enslaved labor, to find gold, and to build a naval base against France
To punish debtors in prison colonies, to spread Catholic missions, and to trade furs
To grow tobacco, to escape religious persecution in Scotland, and to raise cattle
questions.explanation: Historians sum up Georgia's founding as charity, economics, and defense: relieve England's worthy poor, supply the empire with silk, wine, and other products it had to import, and place a soldier-settler shield between South Carolina and Spanish Florida.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Charity, economics, defense - the three reasons for Georgia!

questions.question: Which rule did the Trustees set for Georgia that made it different from every other English colony at first?
questions.correctAnswer: Slavery was banned, along with rum and large land sales
distractors: Only members of the Church of England could own land
Colonists had to pay all taxes in silk cocoons
Women were allowed to vote for the colonial assembly
questions.explanation: The Trustees wanted a colony of small independent farmers who could also serve as soldiers, so they banned slavery, rum, and land speculation. Settlers complained for years that Georgia could not compete with slave-worked South Carolina, and the bans were eventually lifted.
questions.memoryHook: Early Georgia said no to slavery and rum - for a while.

questions.question: Who were the Salzburgers, and what Georgia settlement did they found?
questions.correctAnswer: German-speaking Lutherans fleeing religious persecution in Austria; they founded Ebenezer on the Savannah River
distractors: Scottish soldiers sent to guard the southern border; they founded Darien
Jewish merchants from London; they founded Savannah
French fur traders from Canada; they founded Augusta
questions.explanation: Expelled from Salzburg for their Lutheran faith, the Salzburgers arrived in 1734 and built Ebenezer. They became Georgia's hardest-working farmers and ran its most successful silk production, winding silk cocoons into thread for export.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Salzburgers at Ebenezer - faith, farming, and silk!

questions.question: Why did Oglethorpe recruit the Highland Scots to settle Darien, on Georgia's southern frontier?
questions.correctAnswer: They were famed soldiers who could defend the colony against Spanish Florida
distractors: They were expert silk producers needed at Ebenezer
They were wealthy merchants who financed the colony
They were skilled sailors hired to build Savannah's port
questions.explanation: The Highland Scots who settled Darien in 1736 were recruited as a military colony. Their fighting reputation fit Georgia's buffer role perfectly, and they later fought beside Oglethorpe against Spain in Florida.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Highland Scots at Darien - soldiers on the border!

questions.question: How did the Jewish settlers who arrived in Savannah in 1733 help save the young colony?
questions.correctAnswer: Their physician, Dr. Samuel Nunes, treated colonists through an epidemic that the colony's own doctor could not stop
distractors: They paid off the Trustees' debts to the king
They brought the first enslaved workers to the colony
They negotiated the treaty that ended war with Spain
questions.explanation: When 42 Jewish settlers arrived in July 1733, Savannah was suffering an epidemic and its physician had died. Dr. Samuel Nunes's treatments ended the sickness, and the grateful colony let the group stay despite the Trustees' doubts.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Dr. Nunes cured Savannah's epidemic - the colony kept his people.

questions.question: What major change came to Georgia in 1752 when the Trustees returned the charter to the king?
questions.correctAnswer: Georgia became a royal colony, and the bans on slavery and rum were lifted
distractors: Georgia became an independent republic for ten years
Georgia merged with South Carolina into one colony
All land in Georgia was returned to the Creek Nation
questions.explanation: Frustrated by slow growth, the Trustees gave up a year early. As a royal colony Georgia got a king-appointed governor and an elected assembly, and plantation slavery quickly spread, remaking the colony's economy along the South Carolina model.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 1752 - the king takes over, and slavery becomes legal.

questions.question: Who were Georgia's three signers of the Declaration of Independence?
questions.correctAnswer: Button Gwinnett, Lyman Hall, and George Walton
distractors: James Oglethorpe, Henry Ellis, and James Wright
Elijah Clarke, Nancy Hart, and Austin Dabney
William Few, Abraham Baldwin, and James Jackson
questions.explanation: Georgia, the youngest colony, sent Button Gwinnett, Lyman Hall, and George Walton to sign in 1776. Gwinnett's signature later became one of the rarest and most valuable of all the signers because he died in a duel the next year.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Gwinnett, Hall, and Walton signed for Georgia!

questions.question: Why was the Patriot victory at the Battle of Kettle Creek (1779) so important for Georgia?
questions.correctAnswer: It was Georgia's only major Patriot victory in the state, and it broke the Loyalist militia's momentum after the British captured Savannah
distractors: It forced the British to surrender at Yorktown a month later
It won Georgia control of Florida's ports
It convinced France to join the war on the American side
questions.explanation: In February 1779, Patriot militia under Elijah Clarke and John Dooly surprised and defeated a larger Loyalist force at Kettle Creek. The win kept the backcountry resistance alive at a moment when British forces held Savannah and most of coastal Georgia.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Kettle Creek - small battle, huge lift for Georgia Patriots!

questions.question: What happened at the Siege of Savannah in 1779?
questions.correctAnswer: A combined French and American attack failed to retake Savannah from the British, and Polish hero Casimir Pulaski was killed
distractors: The British surrendered Savannah without firing a shot
American forces burned Savannah to keep it from the French
Georgia's navy captured the entire British fleet in the harbor
questions.explanation: In October 1779 a French fleet and American troops assaulted British-held Savannah and were beaten back with heavy losses. Cavalry commander Casimir Pulaski died of his wounds, and Savannah stayed in British hands until 1782.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Savannah 1779 - the attack failed, and Pulaski fell.

questions.question: Why was Georgia slower than the other colonies to join the revolutionary movement?
questions.correctAnswer: It was the youngest colony, depended on British troops for protection against Spain and Native nations, and many settlers stayed loyal to the king
distractors: Georgia had no ports, so colonists never heard about British taxes
Georgia's leaders were all living in England during the 1770s
Georgia had already won independence from Britain in 1763
questions.explanation: Georgia hesitated because its survival had always rested on Britain: the colony was small, new, and exposed on the frontier. It even skipped the First Continental Congress in 1774, joining the cause only as tensions became impossible to avoid in 1775.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Young, small, and exposed - Georgia joined the revolt late.

questions.question: Georgia was the only colony where the British accomplished what during the Revolutionary War?
questions.correctAnswer: They restored royal government after recapturing the colony's capital and coastal region
distractors: They persuaded the colony to sign a separate peace treaty in 1776
They bought the colony back from the Continental Congress
They freed every enslaved person in the colony permanently
questions.explanation: After taking Savannah in late 1778, the British restored Governor James Wright and royal rule in Georgia - the only place in America where the king's government fully returned. Royal government in Georgia lasted until the British evacuated in 1782.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Only in Georgia did the king's government actually come back.

questions.question: Where in Georgia did Eli Whitney develop the cotton gin in 1793?
questions.correctAnswer: At Mulberry Grove, a plantation near Savannah
distractors: At a mill in the gold town of Dahlonega
At the state capitol in Milledgeville
At a shipyard in Brunswick
questions.explanation: Whitney, a Yale graduate tutoring on Catherine Greene's Mulberry Grove plantation, built a machine that pulled seeds from short-staple cotton fiber. One worker with a gin could clean about fifty times as much cotton as by hand.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The gin was born at Mulberry Grove near Savannah!

questions.question: What was the cotton gin's most important effect on Georgia and the South?
questions.correctAnswer: It made short-staple cotton hugely profitable, which expanded cotton farming and increased the demand for enslaved labor
distractors: It ended slavery by replacing enslaved workers with machines
It made Georgia's main crop rice instead of cotton
It caused cotton prices to collapse and plantations to close
questions.explanation: The gin removed the bottleneck in cleaning cotton, so planters rushed to grow more of it across Georgia's interior. Instead of reducing labor, the invention tied the region's wealth to enslaved workers and pushed hard against Creek and Cherokee land.
questions.memoryHook: The gin meant more cotton - and more enslaved labor.

questions.question: How did Georgia distribute most of the land it took from the Creek and Cherokee nations?
questions.correctAnswer: Through land lotteries that awarded parcels to ordinary white citizens by chance
distractors: By selling every acre to the single highest-bidding land company
By giving all of it to Revolutionary War generals as payment
By keeping it as public hunting land owned by the state
questions.explanation: Between 1805 and 1833 Georgia ran eight land lotteries. For a small fee, eligible citizens - including widows and orphans - could win 40- to 490-acre lots, a system Georgia leaders argued was fairer and less corrupt than selling land to speculators.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Georgia raffled Native land in lotteries, lot by lot.

questions.question: What happened near Dahlonega, Georgia, in 1828-1829?
questions.correctAnswer: Gold was discovered there, setting off the first major gold rush in the United States
distractors: Oil was struck, making Georgia the top oil state
A diamond mine opened that still operates today
The first railroad in the South began running
questions.explanation: The Dahlonega gold discovery drew thousands of miners onto Cherokee land in north Georgia. The rush intensified Georgia's demand to remove the Cherokee, and a U.S. mint branch later opened in Dahlonega to coin the gold.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Gold at Dahlonega - America's first big gold rush!

questions.question: In Worcester v. Georgia (1832), what did the U.S. Supreme Court rule?
questions.correctAnswer: Georgia's laws had no force inside Cherokee territory, because the Cherokee Nation was a distinct community under federal protection
distractors: Georgia could tax the Cherokee for using state roads
The Cherokee had to give up all land east of the Mississippi at once
Missionaries needed Georgia's permission papers to live in the United States
questions.explanation: Chief Justice John Marshall's court sided with missionary Samuel Worcester: only the federal government, not Georgia, could deal with the Cherokee Nation. Georgia refused to obey, the president declined to enforce the ruling, and removal went forward anyway.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Court backed the Cherokee - Georgia ignored it.

questions.question: What name is given to the Cherokee people's forced march from their Georgia homeland to Oklahoma in 1838-1839, during which roughly 4,000 people died?
questions.correctAnswer: The Trail of Tears
distractors: The Long Walk of the Navajo
The Middle Passage
Sherman's March to the Sea
questions.explanation: After the contested Treaty of New Echota, U.S. troops rounded up about 16,000 Cherokee into stockades and forced them west in the winter of 1838-1839. Exposure, disease, and hunger killed roughly 4,000 people on the journey.
questions.memoryHook: The Trail of Tears - a removal Georgia must never forget.

questions.question: How did the Creek (Muscogee) Nation lose most of its Georgia land in the 1820s?
questions.correctAnswer: Through treaties such as Indian Springs (1825), in which Creek leaders ceded the nation's remaining Georgia lands under heavy U.S. and Georgia pressure
distractors: The Creek sold the land willingly to a private railroad company
The Creek abandoned Georgia after losing a war to the Cherokee
A court ruled the Creek had never legally owned any land
questions.explanation: Creek chief William McIntosh signed the Treaty of Indian Springs ceding Creek land in Georgia - a move most Creeks rejected, and McIntosh was executed under Creek law for it. Within a few years the Creek had lost all their Georgia territory.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Indian Springs took the Creek's Georgia land.

questions.question: When did Georgia secede from the Union, and what did it join?
questions.correctAnswer: Georgia seceded in January 1861 and joined the Confederate States of America
distractors: Georgia seceded in 1850 and formed its own independent republic
Georgia never seceded; it stayed neutral through the war
Georgia seceded in 1865, after the war had already ended

questions.question: Why was capturing Atlanta the main goal of General William T. Sherman's 1864 campaign in Georgia?
questions.correctAnswer: Atlanta was the Confederacy's key railroad hub and manufacturing center in the Southeast, so taking it would cripple Confederate supply lines
distractors: Atlanta held the entire Confederate treasury in its banks
Atlanta was the capital of the Confederacy in 1864
Atlanta was Georgia's largest seaport for cotton exports
questions.explanation: Four railroads met in Atlanta, and its factories, foundries, and warehouses fed Confederate armies. When Sherman took the city in September 1864, he cut a supply artery - and the news boosted Lincoln's reelection campaign in the North.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Take the railroad hub, and the Confederacy starves.

questions.question: What strategy did Sherman use on his March to the Sea from Atlanta to Savannah in late 1864?
questions.correctAnswer: His army lived off the land and destroyed railroads, factories, and supplies to break Georgia's ability and will to keep fighting
distractors: His army dug trenches and besieged Savannah for a full year
His army marched only at night and avoided all towns and farms
His army freed Savannah first and then surrendered Atlanta back
questions.explanation: Sherman called it total war: about 62,000 soldiers cut loose from their supply lines, foraged from farms, wrecked rail lines by heating and twisting the rails, and burned military targets. The march showed Georgians the Confederacy could not protect them.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Sherman marched to the sea to break the war machine.

questions.question: What was Andersonville, and why is it remembered as one of the Civil War's darkest sites?
questions.correctAnswer: A Confederate prison camp in southwest Georgia where about 13,000 captured Union soldiers died from disease, crowding, and lack of food and clean water

The battlefield where the Atlanta Campaign began
A Confederate fort that guarded the Savannah River

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Andersonville - 13,000 prisoners never came home.

questions.question: How did the Union blockade affect Georgia during the Civil War?
questions.correctAnswer: It choked off Savannah's trade, so Georgia could not easily export cotton or import manufactured goods and weapons
distractors: It had no effect because Georgia had no coastline
It forced Georgia to build its own navy of ironclad ships
It raised cotton prices so high that Georgia planters grew rich

questions.question: What famous message did Sherman send President Lincoln after reaching Savannah in December 1864?
questions.correctAnswer: He offered Lincoln the city of Savannah as a Christmas gift
distractors: He asked Lincoln for permission to surrender his army
He announced that Atlanta had elected a new mayor
He requested 100,000 more soldiers to attack Florida
questions.explanation: Savannah's defenders evacuated rather than fight, and Sherman wired Lincoln: 'I beg to present you as a Christmas gift the City of Savannah.' The telegram, published in Northern newspapers, proved the march had succeeded and lifted Northern morale.

questions.question: What did the Freedmen's Bureau do in Georgia during Reconstruction?
questions.correctAnswer: It helped formerly enslaved people by opening schools, supervising labor contracts, and providing food, clothing, and medical care
distractors: It returned confiscated plantations to their former owners at once
It organized Georgia's removal of Native Americans to Oklahoma
It sold railroad lines to Northern investors for the U.S. Treasury
questions.explanation: The Bureau's biggest legacy in Georgia was education: it helped found hundreds of schools for Black children and adults who had been forbidden to learn to read. questions.question: Why did Georgia have to be readmitted to the Union twice during Reconstruction?
questions.correctAnswer: After its first readmission, Georgia's legislature expelled its duly elected Black members, so Congress placed the state under military rule again until it seated them and ratified the Fifteenth Amendment
distractors: Georgia's governor forgot to sign the readmission papers the first time
Georgia seceded a second time to join Mexico
Congress lost Georgia's application and asked for a new one

distractors: Georgia may print its own money; the federal government may not
Georgia's budget is written by Congress in Washington
Georgia is forbidden to collect any taxes at all
questions.explanation: Georgia's constitution requires a balanced budget: the governor proposes one and the General Assembly must pass appropriations the state can pay for. The federal government faces no such constitutional rule and regularly runs deficits.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Georgia must balance the books - Washington need not!

questions.question: Georgians ratified their current constitution in 1983. How many constitutions has Georgia had in its history?
questions.correctAnswer: Ten
distractors: Two
Five
Twenty
questions.explanation: Georgia has rewritten its constitution ten times - in 1777, 1789, 1798, 1861, 1865, 1868, 1877, 1945, 1976, and 1983 - far more often than the United States, which still uses its 1787 constitution with amendments.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Ten constitutions - Georgia rewrites, America amends!

img.scene: A row of ten framed parchment documents of different ages displayed on a museum wall from oldest and most faded to newest and crispest, visitors reading below, educational illustration. No legible text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: How can Georgia's constitution be amended?
questions.correctAnswer: The General Assembly proposes an amendment, and Georgia's voters must approve it in a referendum
distractors: The governor may rewrite any section by executive order
Only the U.S. Supreme Court can change it
County governments vote on it without a public election
questions.explanation: An amendment needs two-thirds support in both houses of the General Assembly and then a majority of Georgia voters at the next general election. The process puts the final say with the people, just as ratification did in 1983.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Lawmakers propose, but Georgia voters decide!

img.scene: Voters of many backgrounds casting paper ballots into a ballot box inside a community hall, poll workers at a table nearby, educational illustration. No legible text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: A Georgia citizen believes a new state law violates her rights. Which document should she check first for rights protected specifically at the state level?
questions.correctAnswer: Article I, the Bill of Rights, of the Georgia constitution
distractors: Article II of the U.S. Constitution, about the presidency
The minutes of her county commission meeting
The Georgia Driver's Manual published by the DDS
questions.explanation: Georgia's own Bill of Rights is Article I of the state constitution, and it protects freedoms such as speech, religion, and due process - in some places, like the ban on excessive bail and protection of the press, in Georgia's own words.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Georgia rights live in Article I - check there first!

questions.question: Which qualification must a person meet to vote in Georgia elections?
questions.correctAnswer: Be a U.S. citizen, a legal resident of Georgia and of their county, and at least 18 years old by election day
distractors: Own property in Georgia worth a set minimum amount
Have been born within Georgia's borders
Be at least 25 years old and employed full time
questions.explanation: Georgia's constitution sets the voter qualifications: citizenship, Georgia and county residency, and age 18 - and 17-and-a-half-year-olds may register so they can vote once they turn 18. Felony sentences can suspend the right until completed.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Citizen, resident, eighteen - then you can vote in Georgia!

questions.correctAnswer: A Senate of 56 members and a House of Representatives of 180 members
distractors: A Senate of 100 members and a House of 56 members
A single chamber of 236 members called the Assembly
A Senate of 36 members and a House of 99 members
questions.explanation: The numbers 56 and 180 are worth memorizing for the Georgia Studies test. Members of both houses serve two-year terms and are elected from districts drawn to hold roughly equal populations.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 56 senators, 180 representatives - Georgia's numbers!

questions.question: What are the minimum qualifications to serve in the Georgia Senate?
questions.correctAnswer: At least 25 years old, a U.S. citizen, a Georgia citizen for at least two years, and a resident of the district for at least one year
distractors: At least 21 years old with no citizenship requirement
At least 30 years old and a Georgia resident for ten years
At least 18 years old and a high school graduate
questions.explanation: Georgia senators must be 25; House members need only be 21 - one of the classic comparisons on the state test. Both must be U.S. citizens who have lived in Georgia at least two years and in their district at least one.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Senate at 25, House at 21 - five years apart!

questions.question: How long is a term for members of the Georgia General Assembly, and how long is the regular legislative session?
questions.correctAnswer: Two-year terms; the session runs 40 legislative days beginning in January
distractors: Four-year terms; the session runs all year without a break
Six-year terms; the session runs 90 legislative days
One-year terms; the session runs 10 legislative days in June
questions.explanation: Georgia's is a part-time, citizen legislature: members are elected every two years and meet for 40 legislative days spread across the winter and early spring. The short session is why most Georgia lawmakers hold regular jobs back home.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two-year terms, forty days under the Gold Dome!

questions.question: What happens to most bills introduced in the Georgia General Assembly?
questions.correctAnswer: They are studied and debated in committee, where most bills are changed or stopped before ever reaching a full vote
distractors: They become law automatically after 30 days without a vote
They are sent directly to the governor's desk the same day
They are decided by the Georgia Supreme Court first
questions.explanation: Committees are the legislature's filter: small groups of members hold hearings, hear from citizens and experts, and rewrite or kill most proposals. Only bills that survive committee get debated by the full House or Senate.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Most bills live or die in committee!

questions.question: Who presides over the Georgia Senate, and who presides over the Georgia House of Representatives?
questions.correctAnswer: The lieutenant governor presides over the Senate; the Speaker presides over the House
distractors: The governor presides over both chambers
The chief justice presides over the Senate; the attorney general over the House
The secretary of state presides over both chambers
questions.explanation: Georgia elects its lieutenant governor separately from the governor, and that officer runs the Senate's daily work. House members choose their own leader, the Speaker, from among themselves - one reason the Speaker is so powerful.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Lieutenant governor in the Senate, Speaker in the House!

questions.question: Which list gives the qualifications to become governor of Georgia?
questions.correctAnswer: At least 30 years old, a U.S. citizen for at least 15 years, and a Georgia resident for at least 6 years
distractors: At least 25 years old, a U.S. citizen for 5 years, and a Georgia resident for 1 year
At least 35 years old, born in Georgia, and a former legislator
At least 21 years old with no residency requirement
questions.explanation: The governor's qualifications (30 / 15 / 6) are stricter than a legislator's because the office holds the whole executive branch. A candidate must also be a qualified voter who has not held certain federal or military offices at filing time.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Governor numbers - 30 years old, 15 a citizen, 6 in Georgia!

questions.question: How long is a Georgia governor's term, and how many terms in a row may a governor serve?
questions.correctAnswer: Four-year terms, with a limit of two consecutive terms
distractors: Two-year terms, with no limit on re-election
Six-year terms, with a limit of one term only
Four-year terms, with a lifetime limit of one term
questions.explanation: Like the U.S. president, a Georgia governor can serve eight straight years and then must step aside - though after sitting out a term, a former governor may legally run again. Several Georgia governors have served non-consecutive terms.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Four years a term, two in a row at most!

questions.question: Unlike the U.S. president, who appoints nearly all top executive officials, Georgia's voters directly elect several executive officers. Which are elected separately in Georgia?
questions.correctAnswer: The lieutenant governor, secretary of state, attorney general, state school superintendent, and commissioners such as agriculture, insurance, and labor
distractors: Only the governor is elected; every other officer is appointed
The governor, chief justice, and Speaker of the House
The mayors of the five largest cities in the state
questions.explanation: Georgia's executive branch is deliberately divided: voters choose a whole team of officers, each with defined duties, so the governor cannot control them all. This is a favorite SS8CG3 comparison between Georgia and the federal system.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: In Georgia, voters elect the whole executive team!

questions.question: Which of these is a formal power of Georgia's governor acting as the state's chief executive?
questions.correctAnswer: Signing or vetoing bills passed by the General Assembly
distractors: Declaring Georgia laws unconstitutional
Drawing the boundaries of congressional districts alone
Sentencing criminals convicted in superior court
questions.explanation: The governor's veto is the executive's main check on the legislature; the General Assembly can override it with a two-thirds vote of both houses. Declaring laws unconstitutional belongs to the courts, not the governor.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The governor's pen can sign - or stop - a bill!

questions.question: Georgia's governor has one budget power that the President of the United States does not have. What is it?
questions.correctAnswer: The line-item veto - the power to strike individual spending items from the budget bill without vetoing the whole bill
distractors: The power to collect federal income taxes for the state
The power to set interest rates at Georgia banks
The power to cancel elections during a budget crisis
questions.explanation: When the General Assembly passes the appropriations bill, Georgia's governor may cross out single line items. Presidents have wanted this power for a century, but the U.S. Supreme Court ruled a federal line-item veto unconstitutional in 1998.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Georgia's governor can veto line by line!

The Superior Court of Fulton County, with six judges
The State Court of Georgia, with seven justices
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court of Georgia, expanded to nine justices in 2016, has the final word on Georgia law and reviews cases involving the state constitution, death sentences, and election disputes. Its decisions can be appealed only to the U.S. Supreme Court.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Nine justices top Georgia's court system!

questions.question: How do most judges in Georgia get their jobs, and how is that different from federal judges?
questions.correctAnswer: Georgia judges are elected by the voters in nonpartisan elections; federal judges are appointed by the president and confirmed by the U.S. Senate
distractors: Georgia judges are appointed by the governor for life; federal judges are elected
Georgia judges inherit their positions from family members
Both Georgia and federal judges are chosen by lottery from lawyers
questions.explanation: Nonpartisan means judicial candidates appear on the ballot without party labels, keeping campaigns focused on qualifications. A governor may fill a mid-term vacancy by appointment, but the judge must then face the voters.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Georgia elects its judges; Washington appoints them!

questions.question: What is the main job of the Court of Appeals of Georgia?
questions.correctAnswer: To review decisions from lower trial courts for legal errors, as the state's intermediate appeals court
distractors: To hold the first trial in every criminal case in Georgia
To write new laws when the General Assembly is out of session
To elect the justices of the Georgia Supreme Court
questions.explanation: Most appeals in Georgia stop at the Court of Appeals, which checks whether the trial court applied the law correctly - it does not hold new trials or hear witnesses. Only certain cases go on up to the Supreme Court of Georgia.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Court of Appeals checks trials for legal mistakes!

questions.question: A Georgian is charged with a serious felony and demands a jury trial. In which court will the case be tried?
questions.correctAnswer: A superior court, Georgia's trial court of general jurisdiction
distractors: A probate court, which handles wills and licenses
A magistrate court, which handles small claims
The Georgia Supreme Court, which tries all felonies
questions.explanation: Superior courts are Georgia's main trial courts: they alone try felonies, handle divorce and land-title cases, and hear appeals from lower courts. Georgia is divided into judicial circuits, each with its own superior court judges.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Felonies go to superior court - the big trial court!

questions.question: How does Georgia's juvenile justice system differ from the adult criminal system?
questions.correctAnswer: Its main goal is rehabilitation of the young person, and cases are usually handled in juvenile court for offenders under 17
distractors: It gives children longer sentences than adults for the same acts
It has no judges; parents decide all punishments alone
It applies only to children who have never attended school
questions.explanation: Juvenile court focuses on treatment, counseling, and supervision rather than punishment, and its hearings are closed to protect the child's future. Georgia law does let the most serious violent offenses by 13- to 17-year-olds be tried in superior court as adults.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Juvenile court aims to rehabilitate, not punish!

questions.question: In Georgia juvenile law, what is the difference between a delinquent act and an unruly (status) act?
questions.correctAnswer: A delinquent act would be a crime if committed by an adult; an unruly act, such as truancy or running away, is an offense only because of the child's age or status
distractors: A delinquent act is committed at school; an unruly act is committed at home
A delinquent act is forgiven automatically; an unruly act always means jail
There is no difference; the two terms are exact synonyms
questions.explanation: The distinction matters because an unruly child - a runaway, a truant, a child beyond parental control - has broken no criminal law and cannot be locked up like a delinquent. Georgia courts respond with services and supervision for the family instead.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Delinquent breaks the law; unruly breaks the rules of childhood!

234 counties - the most of any state

questions.question: Georgia counties and cities pay for services such as police, fire protection, water, and road repair mainly with what revenue?

Fees paid directly by the U.S. Congress each month
Selling county land to foreign governments
questions.explanation: The property tax is local government's workhorse because it is stable and tied to local land values. A SPLOST (Special Purpose Local Option Sales Tax) adds one cent of sales tax, but only after county voters approve the exact list of projects it funds.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Property taxes run the county; SPLOST builds the projects!

Interstate highways, bicycle paths, ski lifts, and riverboats

questions.question: Maya buys a $120 jacket with a credit card and pays only the minimum payment each month. Why will the jacket end up costing her much more than $120?
questions.correctAnswer: Interest keeps being charged on the remaining balance, so the debt can grow and take years to pay off, costing far more than the original purchase
distractors: The bank adds a fixed $500 fee to every minimum payment
Minimum payments are illegal, so fines pile up monthly
The card company lowers the credit limit to zero each month
questions.explanation: Credit cards charge high interest - often over 20 percent a year - on whatever balance remains. Paying only the minimum mostly feeds the interest, which is exactly the trap SS8E3 wants Georgia students to recognize before their first card.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Minimum payments feed the interest monster!

questions.question: What is the key difference between a debit card and a credit card?
questions.correctAnswer: A debit card spends money already in your bank account; a credit card borrows money from the card company that you must pay back, possibly with interest
distractors: A debit card works only online; a credit card works only in stores
A debit card is for adults; a credit card is a toy version for teens
A credit card spends your own money; a debit card borrows the bank's
questions.explanation: The two cards look identical but move money in opposite directions. Debit pulls from your balance today; credit builds a bill for tomorrow - and used carefully, it also builds the credit history lenders check later.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Debit is your money now; credit is borrowed money!

questions.question: On a pay stub, what is the difference between gross pay and net pay?
questions.correctAnswer: Gross pay is the total earned before deductions; net pay is the amount actually deposited after taxes and other deductions are taken out
distractors: Gross pay is paid in cash; net pay is paid by check only
Net pay is always larger than gross pay
Gross pay is the employer's profit; net pay is the worker's bonus
questions.explanation: Budgeting from gross pay is a classic beginner's mistake. Taxes, Social Security, and any insurance or retirement contributions come out first, so the net - the 'take-home' - is the number a real budget must use.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Budget with the net - that is what you take home!

questions.question: Which choice follows the 'needs before wants' rule when money is tight?
questions.correctAnswer: Paying the electric bill before buying concert tickets
distractors: Buying a second phone case in a favorite color
Choosing the most expensive sneakers in the store
Ordering dessert after an expensive restaurant meal
questions.explanation: Needs keep you housed, fed, clothed, and connected to work or school; wants make life more fun but can wait. SS8E3 budgeting starts by funding every need before a single want gets a dollar.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Needs first, wants second - that is the rule!

questions.question: Which habit does the most to build a strong credit score over time?
questions.correctAnswer: Paying every bill on time and keeping credit card balances low compared with their limits
distractors: Opening as many new credit cards as possible each month
Borrowing the maximum amount allowed on every card
Never using credit of any kind for your entire life
questions.explanation: Payment history is the largest part of a credit score, and using only a small share of your available credit is next. Lenders read the score as a trust report - steady, on-time, low-balance behavior is what earns cheaper loans later.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Pay on time, keep balances low - your score grows!

questions.question: Why do people buy insurance, such as car or health insurance?
questions.correctAnswer: To protect themselves from large financial losses by paying a smaller, predictable premium that shares risk across many people
distractors: To earn a guaranteed profit every year they stay healthy
Because the government keeps all insurance payments in savings accounts
To avoid ever paying for any repair or medical bill themselves
questions.explanation: Insurance trades an unknown, possibly ruinous cost for a known, affordable one. The insurer pools premiums from many customers, knowing only some will file claims - the risk-management idea at the heart of SS8E3's money-management principles.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Insurance turns one big risk into many small payments!
